_doc: Phase 379. One row per item where the nano-ros user API does NOT correspond
to the ROS 2 client library it mirrors. Written by hand; read by
`scripts/api-parity.py --check`, which fails on any non-matching row that has
no entry here.
Key is '<lang>:<normalized item>' exactly as the report prints it, where lang
is one of c / cpp / rust. Run the report to get the spelling; do not guess it.
verdict is one of:
divergence  we changed it and a PLATFORM CONSTRAINT is why. `why` must name
the constraint (no_std, no exceptions, no allocator, no runtime
env, single-threaded transport) -- not a preference. This is the
only sanctioned reason to differ (RFC-0036).
extension   we add it because an RTOS scenario needs it; ROS 2 has none.
declined    ROS 2 has it, we deliberately do not, with the reason.
gap         ROS 2 has it, we should too, nobody has done it. A gap is a
legitimate entry -- the point is that it is written down.
rename      the names differ and OURS is the one that should change. A
rename with no platform reason costs the drop-in claim for
nothing, so these are the campaign's work list.
This file is SEEDED, not complete: W1 shipped the correlator, W2 classifies
the rest. `--check` is deliberately not wired into `just check` until then --
a gate that fails on ~2000 rows from the day it lands is one somebody
switches off. Keys beginning with '_' are documentation and are skipped.
the `<lang>:` rows for its own lane, and `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every
shard in this directory. One agent per lane can write without a rebase
conflict against the others.
SHARDED BY TOPIC: this file holds one stage's rows in ALL THREE
languages, because the campaign closes a feature at a time across every
language. `scripts/api-parity.py` merges every shard here, and
`--self-test` rejects a row whose item belongs to a different stage.

c:deadline_policy_t.why: not a QoS policy at all, despite the name. `nros_deadline_policy_t` (RELEASED / ACTIVATED / INHERITED) is RFC-0047's real-time SCHEDULING deadline interpretation -- a field of `nros_sched_context_t`, mirroring `nros_node::executor::sched_context::DeadlinePolicy`. The RTOS scenario is a periodic task whose deadline is measured from release, from activation, or inherited from its caller; rcl has no scheduling context so ROS 2 has nothing to compare it with. It appears in this stage because `topics.py`'s KEY_OVERRIDES maps `deadline_policy_t` to qos while its three siblings `sched_class_t`, `sched_priority_t` and `sched_context_t` map to exec -- the verdict is right, the shard is not.

c:executor_add_client_with_request_id.why: rclc ships a second registration entry point whose callback also receives the `rmw_request_id_t`. Ours has one registration verb: the correlation token is an `int64_t` sequence number that `nros_client_send_request` returns and `nros_service_send_response` takes back (see the service stage's `cpp:Client::create_request_header`), and it belongs to the ENTITY, not to a second `add_*` overload. A registration entry point per callback shape is the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule seen from the executor's side.

c:executor_add_service_with_context.why: every nano-ros callback typedef already ends in `void *context`, and the pair is bound to the ENTITY at creation (RFC-0041/0043) rather than handed to the executor. So `nros_executor_add_service` IS rclc's with-context form -- rclc needs the variant only because its base callback has no context parameter. See `c:subscription_callback_t`.

c:executor_bind_handle_to_sched_context.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. This is the primitive the group table is built on: bind one registered handle to one SchedContext, applied on the next spin cycle.

c:executor_create_sched_context.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. Registers one SchedContext (class + priority + period/budget/deadline) into the executor's fixed `NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_SC` table; `NROS_RET_FULL` when it is exhausted.

c:executor_default_sched_context_id.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. The auto-created FIFO context every unbound callback maps to, so 'no scheduling opinion' is a real value rather than a null.

c:executor_get_handle_count.why: how many arena slots are in use. The arena is a compile-time-sized table (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`), so 'did my registrations fit?' is a real question with a cheap answer; rclc answers it only by failing the next `add_*`. See `c:executor_get_remaining_handles`.

c:executor_get_remaining_handles.why: the other half of `c:executor_get_handle_count`: remaining arena capacity, asked BEFORE registering. An image that registers entities conditionally at boot (a sensor that may or may not be present) needs to know whether the optional set still fits, rather than discovering it from a `NROS_RET_FULL` halfway through bring-up.

c:executor_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our naming; see `c:publisher_get_zero_initialized`.

c:executor_get_zero_initialized_executor.why: rclc's stuttering spelling -- the type name appears twice. Ours is `nros_executor_get_zero_initialized`, the method-style name on the type. See `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`.

c:executor_has_param.why: 'is this parameter declared?', asked without the six `rcl_interfaces/srv/*` servers being up. Parameters live on the EXECUTOR here rather than on a node (see the param stage's `c:executor_register_parameter_services`), and a device that bakes its parameter set (RFC-0045) wants a local existence check that costs no queryable slot -- `ZPICO_MAX_QUERYABLES` is 8 on embedded (issue 0460).

c:executor_invocation_t.why: ours drops `handle_` from rclc's `rclc_executor_handle_invocation_t`; the values are the same pair (`ON_NEW_DATA` / `ALWAYS`) and the meaning is identical. The theirs-only half is filtered out of the report as plumbing, so this row carries both sides. No platform reason -- the shorter name costs a C user the rclc spelling for nothing. Phase 379 W5.

c:executor_is_valid.why: mirrors `rcl_context_is_valid` on the object that actually holds the session here; see `c:support_is_valid`. rclc ships no `rclc_executor_is_valid`.

c:executor_node_init.why: static entity storage plus one session: a node is created ON the executor (`nros_executor_node_init(executor, node, name, options)`) and lands in the executor's node table (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_NODES`), so it cannot exist before one or be moved between two. rcl builds a node from an `rcl_context_t` and rclc adds it nowhere; see `cpp:Executor::add_node` for the same divergence in C++ and `cpp:Context` for why there is no separate context.

c:executor_ping.why: wire-level round trip -- is the XRCE agent / zenoh router still reachable, within `timeout_ms`. Mirrors micro-ROS's `rmw_uros_ping_agent`, which rclc has no counterpart for. The scenario is reconnect-on-link-loss: a device on a flaky radio has to distinguish 'nobody is publishing' from 'the session is dead' and re-open, and neither returns an error from `spin_some`.

c:executor_prepare.why: rclc pre-allocates its `rcl_wait_set` from the handles registered so far, so a later `spin` does not allocate. There is no wait set (rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.) and the arena is sized at compile time, so there is nothing to pre-allocate: static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated.

c:executor_remove_*.why: rclc can drop a subscription, client, service, timer or guard condition from a spinning executor. static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated. What a user loses: retiring an entity at runtime to reclaim its slot -- a mode change has to register every entity it may ever need at boot and gate them, which is also what a memory budget that must be known before flashing wants. This is a deliberate shape, not an oversight; if it is ever wanted, slot reuse needs handle generation counters first.

c:executor_state_t.why: an explicit executor lifecycle (uninitialised / initialised / spinning / shutdown) so a double-init or a use-after-fini is a returned code rather than undefined behaviour on a device that cannot report a crash. See `c:support_state_t`. Note the SPINNING state is the only place in the tree that models `rclcpp::Executor::is_spinning` -- and it is not exported; see `cpp:Executor::is_spinning`.

c:executor_stop.why: stop a spinning executor WITHOUT finalizing it -- flips `nros_executor_state_t` back from SPINNING to INITIALIZED so `nros_executor_spin`'s loop exits and the session stays open for a later spin. rclc's `rclc_executor_spin` has no way out at all. The scenario is a mode change on an RTOS task (safe-state, OTA staging) where tearing the middleware down and re-opening it costs a full discovery round. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: this capability is spelled three ways and one language does not have it: C `nros_executor_stop`, Rust `Executor::halt` / `is_halted` / `halt_flag`, rclcpp `Executor::cancel` -- and C++ has NOTHING, because `Executor::spin` there exits only on `shutdown()`, which calls `nros_cpp_fini` and destroys the session. See `cpp:Executor::cancel`.

c:get_zero_initialized_guard_condition.why: rcl's free-function zero-init spelling; ours is `nros_guard_condition_get_zero_initialized`. See `c:get_zero_initialized_publisher`.

c:get_zero_initialized_wait_set.why: there is no wait-set type to zero-initialize. rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.

c:guard_condition_callback_t.why: the callback type belongs to the guard condition rather than to the executor's `add` call, because it is bound to the entity (RFC-0041). rcl's counterpart is the `rclc_gc_callback_t` passed to `rclc_executor_add_guard_condition` -- the `executor-owns-no-entity-storage` rule, seen as a type. See `c:subscription_callback_t`.

c:guard_condition_clear.why: clear the triggered flag; the other half of `c:guard_condition_is_triggered`, and absent from C++ and Rust for the same reason recorded there.

c:guard_condition_get_default_options.why: no runtime options struct: QoS and entity options are compile-time (RFC-0036/0045). See the `compile-time-options` signature rule.

c:guard_condition_get_options.why: no runtime options struct: QoS and entity options are compile-time (RFC-0036/0045). See the `compile-time-options` signature rule.

c:guard_condition_get_rmw_handle.why: our RMW seam is the vtable (RFC-0035), not an entity accessor. See `c:node_get_rmw_handle`.

c:guard_condition_get_zero_initialized.why: rcl's zero-init idiom under our naming; see `c:publisher_get_zero_initialized`.

c:guard_condition_impl_t.why: rcl's pimpl; our handles carry their state inline. See `c:publisher_impl_t`.

c:guard_condition_init_from_rmw.why: adopts an already-constructed `rmw_guard_condition_t`. our RMW seam is the vtable (RFC-0035), not an entity accessor. See `c:node_get_rmw_handle`. There is no rmw-level object for a caller to hold, so there is nothing to adopt.

c:guard_condition_is_triggered.why: read the triggered flag without consuming it. The scenario is the RFC-0022 polling tier: a task that owns its own loop and never calls a callback still needs to see the flag an ISR set. rcl has no reader -- a wait set is the only way to observe an rcl guard condition. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: C ships `is_triggered` + `clear`, C++ ships neither (only `trigger` and `is_valid`), and Rust's `GuardConditionHandle` ships only `trigger`. A polling C++ or Rust user cannot do what a polling C user can.

c:guard_condition_options_t.why: no runtime options struct: QoS and entity options are compile-time (RFC-0036/0045). See the `compile-time-options` signature rule.

c:guard_condition_set_callback.why: RFC-0041/0043 bind a callback to the ENTITY, and in C the binding is a SEPARATE call after `nros_guard_condition_init` -- which is exactly the after-the-fact installation shape we decline in C++ at `cpp:GuardCondition::set_on_trigger_callback`. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: the guard condition is created three different ways, from three different owners, with three different callback bindings: C `nros_guard_condition_init(guard, SUPPORT)` then `nros_guard_condition_set_callback(...)`; C++ `NODE.create_guard_condition(out, cb, ctx)`, one call, callback at creation; Rust `EXECUTOR.register_guard_condition(closure)` returning `(HandleId, GuardConditionHandle)`. rclcpp constructs one free-standing from a `Context`. Nothing about no_std picks between these -- W5 has to pick one.

c:guard_condition_trigger.why: the ours-only half of `c:trigger_guard_condition`; recorded so the pair is visible from both sides. Thread-safe and lock-free -- it stores into an atomic flag in the executor's arena and then fires the runtime wake hook, so an ISR or a foreign task can release a `spin_once` already blocked in `drive_io`.

c:sched_class_t.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. The queue-and-selection policy: Fifo / Edf / Sporadic / BestEffort / TimeTriggered.

c:sched_context_id_t.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. A `uint8_t` index into the executor's SchedContext table, not a pointer -- the table is static and an id survives being copied into an options struct before the context exists.

c:sched_context_t.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. The context itself.

c:sched_priority_t.why: RFC-0002 section 4.2 / RFC-0047 / RFC-0079 -- the SchedContext surface, which ROS 2 has no counterpart for at all. A mixed-criticality image runs a 20 ms control loop and best-effort telemetry on ONE executor on ONE RTOS task, so the criticality ordering has to live in user space: N callbacks must not cost N kernel priority slots (RFC-0002 non-goal 3), and RFC-0079 exists because the raw kernel number is unwritable by hand -- each RTOS has its own range and its own DIRECTION. rclcpp's nearest answer is one `MultiThreadedExecutor` thread per priority, which an MCU cannot pay for. The criticality BUCKET (Critical / Normal / BestEffort), deliberately three values and not a kernel number: RFC-0079 exists because a raw priority is unwritable by hand across Zephyr (counts down), FreeRTOS and NuttX (count up).

c:trigger_guard_condition.why: rcl's free-function spelling of a verb our C already has method-style (`nros_guard_condition_trigger`). Same shape as `c:publish` and `c:send_response`: the WORD matches, the spelling is ours to align. Phase 379 W5.

c:wait.why: `rcl_wait` -- the blocking call at the centre of the protocol. rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`. Ours is `nros_executor_spin_some(executor, timeout_ns)`, which drives I/O through the RMW vtable and dispatches every ready arena entry in one pass.

c:wait_set_*.why: rcl's wait set; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.

c:wake_state_t.why: caller-declared storage for one wake callback's `(fn, ctx)` pair, passed into `nros_*_set_wake_callback` and kept alive at the same address while the entity is polling. It exists because there is no allocator to put a closure in: the caller declares the slot next to the entity. See the pubsub stage's `c:subscription_set_wake_callback` for the capability itself.

cpp:AnyExecutable.why: An rclcpp internal, not user API -- it is the wait-set result type its executors pass between themselves. A user writes neither the type nor its fields. RFC-0002's executor is not built from it.

cpp:CallbackGroup::CallbackGroup.why: ours is `CallbackGroup(const char* name)`, theirs is `CallbackGroup(CallbackGroupType, bool automatically_add_to_executor_with_node)` -- two arguments each and nothing in common, which is why the correlator calls it arity-only. rclcpp's `CallbackGroupType` is a CONCURRENCY policy -- `MutuallyExclusive` or `Reentrant` -- and it only means anything to a multi-threaded executor deciding whether two callbacks from one group may run at once. RFC-0002 puts one executor on one RTOS task with non-preemptive run-to-completion dispatch, so every group is mutually exclusive by construction and `Reentrant` is unrepresentable: there is no second thread to be reentrant from. The axis our group carries instead is a NAME that `system.toml` maps to a scheduling tier (RFC-0047, RFC-0079) -- the thing a mixed-criticality image actually needs from grouping. `automatically_add_to_executor_with_node` (rclcpp's second constructor argument) is meaningless for the same reason as `cpp:Executor::add_node`.

cpp:CallbackGroup::automatically_add_to_.why: the flag that decides whether an executor picks this group up when its node is added. Nodes are created BY the executor here and are never added to one; see `cpp:Executor::add_node`.

cpp:CallbackGroup::can_be_taken_from.why: the mutual-exclusion latch a multi-threaded executor sets while one of the group's callbacks runs. rclcpp's `CallbackGroupType` is a CONCURRENCY policy -- `MutuallyExclusive` or `Reentrant` -- and it only means anything to a multi-threaded executor deciding whether two callbacks from one group may run at once. RFC-0002 puts one executor on one RTOS task with non-preemptive run-to-completion dispatch, so every group is mutually exclusive by construction and `Reentrant` is unrepresentable: there is no second thread to be reentrant from. The axis our group carries instead is a NAME that `system.toml` maps to a scheduling tier (RFC-0047, RFC-0079) -- the thing a mixed-criticality image actually needs from grouping. `automatically_add_to_executor_with_node` (rclcpp's second constructor argument) is meaningless for the same reason as `cpp:Executor::add_node`.

cpp:CallbackGroup::collect_all_ptrs.why: rclcpp's wait-set protocol; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.

cpp:CallbackGroup::find_waitable_ptrs_if.why: rclcpp's wait-set protocol; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`.

cpp:CallbackGroup::get_associated_with_e.why: the 'already claimed by an executor' atomic, which exists because an rclcpp group can be added to at most one executor at a time. Ours binds at registration into one executor's arena and never moves. RFC-0047: a callback group here is a NAME, not an object the executor holds. The group structure is declared in code (`Node::create_callback_group("ctrl")`) and the group -> tier POLICY is declared in the workspace `system.toml`; the executor carries a config-seeded `group -> sched_context` table and binds each callback to its group's context at REGISTRATION, once, into a fixed arena. There is no group object to add to or remove from an executor, and no membership that can change after registration.

cpp:CallbackGroup::get_name.why: reads the group name back. In RFC-0047 the NAME is the binding -- it is what `system.toml` maps to a tier -- so a helper that forwards a group to `create_timer_in` needs to read it. rclcpp identifies a group by pointer and has no name to read.

cpp:CallbackGroup::get_notify_guard_cond.why: rclcpp wakes a blocked `rcl_wait` when a group's membership changes, so the wait set can be rebuilt. rclcpp's wait-set protocol; the reason is stated in full at `cpp:WaitSet`. Membership is also fixed at registration here (static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated.), so there is no change to notify anyone of.

cpp:CallbackGroup::make_shared.why: no allocator -- one global `nros_platform_alloc` and inline caller-owned storage. See `cpp:Node::make_shared` and the `no-shared-ptr` rule in signature_rules.py. Ours is a value-typed token holding a `const char*`; there is nothing to share.

cpp:CallbackGroupType.why: rclcpp's `CallbackGroupType` is a CONCURRENCY policy -- `MutuallyExclusive` or `Reentrant` -- and it only means anything to a multi-threaded executor deciding whether two callbacks from one group may run at once. RFC-0002 puts one executor on one RTOS task with non-preemptive run-to-completion dispatch, so every group is mutually exclusive by construction and `Reentrant` is unrepresentable: there is no second thread to be reentrant from. The axis our group carries instead is a NAME that `system.toml` maps to a scheduling tier (RFC-0047, RFC-0079) -- the thing a mixed-criticality image actually needs from grouping. `automatically_add_to_executor_with_node` (rclcpp's second constructor argument) is meaningless for the same reason as `cpp:Executor::add_node`.

cpp:Executor::add_callback_group.why: RFC-0047: a callback group here is a NAME, not an object the executor holds. The group structure is declared in code (`Node::create_callback_group("ctrl")`) and the group -> tier POLICY is declared in the workspace `system.toml`; the executor carries a config-seeded `group -> sched_context` table and binds each callback to its group's context at REGISTRATION, once, into a fixed arena. There is no group object to add to or remove from an executor, and no membership that can change after registration.

cpp:Executor::add_node.why: an rclcpp node is standalone and is ATTACHED to an executor, which is what makes it movable between executors and spinnable by more than one. static entity storage: the executor's entity table is an arena sized at compile time (`NROS_EXECUTOR_MAX_HANDLES`) with no allocator behind it, and a `HandleId` is an index into it. Registration is one-way -- no slot is ever reclaimed and no handle is ever invalidated. A node's entities are allocated in the arena of the executor that created it (`cpp:Executor::create_node`), so attachment is not a separate step and cannot be undone. What a user loses: handing an already-built node to a different executor.

cpp:Executor::cancel.why: rclcpp's 'stop spinning, keep everything alive', typically from a signal handler. C++ cannot do it: `Executor::spin` loops while `initialized_` is true and only `shutdown()` clears that, and `shutdown()` calls `nros_cpp_fini` -- so the only way to leave a C++ `spin()` is to destroy the middleware session. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: C has `nros_executor_stop` (SPINNING -> INITIALIZED, session intact) and Rust has `Executor::halt` / `halt_flag` (an atomic a signal handler or another thread sets, plus a wake so a blocked `drive_io` falls through). Nothing about no_std stops C++ from having the same flag; nobody has done it. Phase 379 W3.

cpp:Executor::create.why: no allocator: `Executor` is constructed into CALLER storage -- `nros::Executor exec; Executor::create(exec, locator, domain_id)` -- with the session held in an `alignas(8) uint8_t storage_[NROS_CPP_EXECUTOR_STORAGE_SIZE]` inline array sized by the build. rclcpp's executors are constructed normally and shared by `SharedPtr`. Same shape as the pubsub stage's `cpp:Publisher::Publisher<M>`. the executor IS the session and the context here. `Executor::create` opens the middleware connection, nodes are created ON it, and every entity lands in its arena; there is no `rclcpp::Context` to hold, register with, or shut down separately. See `cpp:Context`.

cpp:Executor::create_node.why: static entity storage plus one session: a node is created BY the executor and its entities live in that executor's arena, so it cannot exist before one. rclcpp constructs a `Node` from a `Context` and later hands it to an executor with `add_node`. See `cpp:Executor::add_node` for the declined half and `c:executor_node_init` for the same divergence in C.

cpp:Executor::get_all_callback_groups.why: RFC-0047: a callback group here is a NAME, not an object the executor holds. The group structure is declared in code (`Node::create_callback_group("ctrl")`) and the group -> tier POLICY is declared in the workspace `system.toml`; the executor carries a config-seeded `group -> sched_context` table and binds each callback to its group's context at REGISTRATION, once, into a fixed arena. There is no group object to add to or remove from an executor, and no membership that can change after registration. There is no registry to enumerate, and no allocator for the `std::vector<WeakPtr>` the enumeration returns.

cpp:Executor::get_automatically_added_ca.why: see `cpp:Executor::get_all_callback_groups`; the automatic/manual distinction is the `automatically_add_to_executor_with_node` flag, declined at `cpp:CallbackGroup::automatically_add_to_executor_with_node`.

cpp:Executor::handle.why: hands back the raw inline storage pointer so the generated C entry points and the C-shaped FFI (`nros_cpp_*`) can reach the same executor a C++ user holds. It exists because the storage IS the object -- there is no pimpl and no allocator to hide one in. rclcpp needs no equivalent because a `SharedPtr` is already the shared identity. See `cpp:Node::executor_handle`.

cpp:Executor::is_spinning.why: rclcpp reports whether a spin is in progress. OUR LANGUAGES DISAGREE: C models the state (`nros_executor_state_t::NROS_EXECUTOR_STATE_SPINNING`, which `nros_executor_stop` reads) but exports no accessor for it; Rust answers the inverse question, `Executor::is_halted`; C++ has neither -- `Executor::ok()` means 'initialised'. Three surfaces, three different answers to one question, and the C++ one is missing. Phase 379 W3.
